topic: Rust (Axum) vs Go (Fiber) vs ASP.NET (Minimal API) — Microservice Backend Benchmark 2026
overall_framing: Go Fiber wins on raw throughput and latency. Rust wins on memory and latency predictability. ASP.NET struggles to justify its 20x memory cost against a 2026 field that has caught up and surpassed it on performance. The 2026 backend question is no longer 'is Rust fast?' — it's 'why is ASP.NET using 357 MB for a microservice that Go runs in 37 MB?'

category_winners.evidence: 28,945 RPS at c=50 vs 11,364 (Rust) and 24,474 (dotnet). At c=200 and c=500, Go maintains 29k RPS while dotnet drops to 14k. Go is 2.55x faster than Rust and 2.06x faster than dotnet under sustained load.

Rust stddev at c=200 is 1.28ms. Go is 0.67ms avg but Rust's worst-case (47ms max) is tighter than dotnet's 956ms max. Under stress (c=500), Rust max is 58ms vs dotnet's 1010ms. For SLA-driven systems, Rust's tail latency is more predictable than either competitor.
category_winners.margin: moderate vs Go, large vs dotnet

category_winners.evidence: 8.2 MB idle, 17.4 MB under c=200 load. Go uses 2.1x more (36.7 MB). ASP.NET uses 20.5x more (356.6 MB) under the same load. At 100 instances: Rust = 1.7 GB, Go = 3.7 GB, dotnet = 35.7 GB.
303ms cold build. dotnet: 835ms. Rust: 45,887ms (151x slower than Go). For teams iterating fast, Rust's compile time is a real productivity tax.
category_winners.margin: massive vs Rust, moderate vs dotnet

category_winners.evidence: 9,093 RPS vs 8,720 (Rust) vs 8,632 (dotnet). All three are within 5% — DB insert latency dominates at this scale. No meaningful winner.
Both hit 89ms. dotnet is 288ms (3.2x slower) due to JIT compilation.
category_winners.margin: tie between Rust/Go; both beat dotnet

category_winners.evidence: 4.1 MB self-contained binary. Go: 20.3 MB (includes runtime). dotnet: 1.6 MB DLL but requires 200+ MB .NET runtime installed on host.
category_winners.margin: Rust smallest self-contained; dotnet misleading without runtime

per_target.name: rust-axum
strengths: Lowest memory: 8.2 MB idle, 17.4 MB under load — 20x less than dotnet
Tightest latency distribution at high concurrency — 58ms max at c=500
Smallest self-contained binary (4.1 MB) — ideal for containers
Zero runtime overhead — no GC pauses, no JIT warmup
Compile-time correctness — memory safety without garbage collection
weaknesses: 45.9 second cold build time — 151x slower than Go
267 dependencies for a basic microservice — supply chain surface area
Read throughput 2.55x lower than Go Fiber — fasthttp has a structural advantage
Higher developer onboarding cost — Rust's borrow checker is a real barrier
Async model (Tokio) requires understanding of futures, pinning, lifetimes
best_for: Services where tail latency SLAs matter (p99 < 100ms under stress)
Teams that can absorb the learning curve and build time
Container-heavy deployments where image size is billing-relevant
Safety-critical infrastructure where memory bugs are unacceptable
avoid_unless: Your team has Rust experience or budget to acquire it
You have CI caching in place — 45s clean builds will kill developer flow
Read throughput is not your primary metric

per_target.name: go-fiber
strengths: 28,945 RPS read throughput — 2.55x faster than Rust on GET workloads
6.87ms avg latency at c=200 — 2.6x better than Rust
Latency flat from c=50 to c=500 — goroutines scale beautifully
Simple concurrency model — goroutines + channels beats async/await for readability
Strong ecosystem for microservices (k8s, observability, gRPC)
weaknesses: 2.1x more memory than Rust under load (36.7 MB vs 17.4 MB)
Fiber uses fasthttp which is not standard net/http — some middleware incompatibility
GC does exist but at these workloads it doesn't appear — may surface at higher loads
Less type safety than Rust — runtime panics are possible
best_for: High-throughput read APIs where latency and RPS are the primary metrics
Teams wanting fast iteration AND strong performance
Microservices in K8s where memory is managed but throughput matters
Anyone coming from a backend team needing strong hiring pool
avoid_unless: You specifically need the lowest possible memory footprint (use Rust then)
You need sub-10ms p99 latency at c=500+ (Rust wins on tail latency)

per_target.name: dotnet-minimal
strengths: Strong at low concurrency: 24,474 RPS at c=50 — close to Go
Write throughput tied with Rust/Go at c=50
Fastest developer productivity for .NET teams — C# is expressive
Largest ecosystem: NuGet, Entity Framework, SignalR, strong Azure integration
Strong tooling: Visual Studio, Rider, dotnet CLI
Best enterprise hiring pool of the three
weaknesses: 356 MB RAM under load — 20x Rust, 9.7x Go. Unacceptable for high-density microservices
Latency spikes to 956ms max at c=200 — GC pauses create p99 landmines
Performance cliff at c=200+: drops from 24k to 14k RPS while competitors hold steady
Requires .NET runtime on host or in container — true deploy size is 200+ MB
Latency stddev of 93ms at c=200 — unpredictable under load
best_for: .NET shops already invested in the ecosystem (Azure, SQL Server, EF Core)
Internal tooling and CRUD services with low concurrency (<50 users)
Teams where developer productivity and C# expertise outweigh operational cost
Services co-located with Azure where .NET runtime cost is amortized
avoid_unless: You're already a .NET shop — the memory and GC costs are hard to justify from scratch in 2026
Concurrency is expected to stay low (<100 simultaneous users)
You have budget to throw memory at the problem

confidence_notes: All numbers measured on real hardware with real PostgreSQL against identical specs. 5 measurement runs per phase. Memory measured both at idle and under sustained c=200 load. Build times are wall-clock. The only uncertainty is that macOS is not a production server environment — Linux would likely show higher absolute RPS for all targets but the relative differences should hold.
caveats: Benchmarks ran on macOS Apple Silicon (M-series), not Linux x86-64. Absolute numbers will differ on Linux — relative rankings expected to hold.
Connection pool capped at 20 connections for all targets (fairness). Error rates at c=500 reflect DB pool exhaustion, not server failures.
dotnet was run with standard JIT (no AOT). AOT compilation would improve startup time and reduce memory but was not tested — it would require separate build configuration.
Go Fiber uses fasthttp, not standard net/http. Standard net/http Go would show lower throughput (~40-50% lower). Fiber's performance advantage over Rust Axum is partly architectural.
Rust build time measured with LTO + codegen-units=1. Disabling LTO would cut build time significantly but reduce peak performance.

POST workload showed high email collision errors in mixed scenarios — POST benchmarks ran with fresh unique email generation but timestamp granularity caused some conflicts. POST RPS numbers reflect realistic collision pressure.
This benchmark does not test Rust's correctness advantages, which are unquantifiable but real.
